items.article_context_en: The venture investor behind early bets on Coinbase, Solana and Uniswap said is broadening its focus, joining other crypto investment firms looking beyond blockchain to artificial intelligence and tech themes. Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), one of crypto's most influential venture capital backers, is dropping "crypto" from the name of its investment arm and expanding into artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies, becoming the latest major crypto investor to broaden its focus. The Silicon Valley firm is renaming its a16z Crypto fund to a16z Frontier, targeting startups developing technologies and markets that may take years to mature, general partner Chris Dixon said in a Thursday blog post. The move doesn't mean a16z is abandoning digital assets. The firm will continue backing crypto companies and advocating for crypto regulation, Dixon said. "This is an expansion: we will continue to invest in crypto and related ventures and advocate for sensible crypto regulation," he wrote. The VC giant had played a significant role in shaping the crypto industry. An early Coinbase investor, the firm also backed major blockchain projects including Solana (SOL) and decentralized exchange Uniswap (UNI), while pouring billions into crypto startups and becoming a prominent voice in U.S. The company’s decision is the latest example of a broader pivot among venture capital firms that made their names in crypto but are now looking beyond digital assets. Paradigm raised $1.2 billion in July to invest in AI, robotics and other technologies, while Framework Ventures raised $400 million in June to expand into AI, energy, fintech and tokenization. Haun Ventures also broadened its focus toward AI and financial services with a $1 billion fundraising in May. A16z Frontier will explore AI-powered products, autonomous machines and networks connecting people and AI agents. Dixon sees blockchains playing a role in those networks by enabling payments and transactions between machines. Dixon argued that as blockchain technology spreads into mainstream finance, the distinction between crypto companies and other businesses is becoming less useful.

items.article_context_en: Leader in cryptocurrency, Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, blockchain, DeFi, digital finance and Web 3.0 news with analysis, video and live price updates. Then, in “Ask an Expert,” Sam Boboev of Fintech WrapUp on whether euro stablecoins can challenge the dollar’s lead, and who is best placed to win on distribution. A year ago, the stablecoin debate centered on whether regulatory clarity and a compelling combination of speed, cost and liquidity benefits would drive meaningful adoption. The evidence now points to a market moving decisively from experimentation toward implementation. EY-Parthenon’s 2026 Blockchain Payments Survey of 521 corporate and financial institution decision-makers found that 18% of corporates have used stablecoins in production, double the share reported in our 2025 survey. Tokenized deposits are close behind, with 15% of corporates reporting adoption. Financial institutions are also making firm commitments. A total of 69% offer stablecoin services or plan to launch them within two years, up from 30% in 2025. Among banks, 49% already offer or plan to offer tokenized deposits over the same period. Although blockchain payments have not yet reached mass adoption, the survey findings provide clear evidence that the market is shifting from technology trials to integrating capabilities into existing payment workflows and treasury operations. Cross-border business payments remain the most common use case. Across stablecoins and tokenized deposits, 50% to 53% of all respondents have used or are exploring each for cross-border supplier payments or cross-border business-to-business (B2B) payment acceptance. Cross-border B2B flows lead blockchain payment use cases for most respondents, while interest in payouts is concentrated among banks and payments firms. These applications directly address frictions corporates experience in cross-border payments.

items.article_context_en: The company is in talks with Visa over a potential $2.5 billion acquisition, Axios reported. Cryptocurrency custody firm Fireblocks dismissed reports it is in talks with Visa (V) to be acquired for $2.5 billion. Axios, citing multiple unidentified sources, said the company was in late-stage talks with Visa. “We are aware of the rumors about a possible acquisition of Fireblocks by Visa. This is news to us, and not true at present time,” a Fireblocks spokesperson said soon after the Axios story broke. Fireblocks specializes in crypto custody using advanced pre-key sharding technologies such as multi-party computation (MPC). A $2.5 billion purchase would be a marked drop in value since 2022, when Fireblocks raised $550 million at an $8 billion valuation. That said, smoke has been circulating over the past three or four weeks about a potential sale of the business, with anonymous sources telling CoinDesk U.S.-listed Coinbase Global COIN$167,98 was also in the frame to buy Fireblocks. After this story was published, Coinbase denied it was involved in a possible transaction. Visa did not respond to requests for comment. 22, 15:24 UTC): Adds Coinbase denial in final paragraph. items.article_context_en: Boosters often say crypto voters can swing elections, but Democrats are seeking mileage out of tying crypto to Trump, corruption and attempts to buy seats in Congress. Crypto is finally being talked about in U.S. political campaigns, but it's certainly not in a light that the industry would choose. Though digital assets advocates have long referenced a grassroots uprising of crypto-focused voters that can swing elections, the industry's own massive campaign spending has carefully decided against even mentioning the financial technology in the ads it buys for favored candidates. But crypto is having a moment in the midterms, anyway, as the sector's critics paint its political involvement as a venal influence on congressional campaigning. A number of Democratic candidates have raised crypto as a black mark to suggest improper corporate sway over their political adversaries and more generally as a factor in corruption accusations against President Donald Trump and his administration. In this environment, in which voters are now weighing government corruption as a top political concern, it may carry consequential weight. In a current campaign ad from Senator Mark Warner, the Virginia Democrat seeks to tarnish Trump and his allies by highlighting the billions Trump has made in office and the jet he accepted as a gift from Qatar. The ad also notes that Trump made hundreds of millions of dollars off of his "crypto memecoin," followed by Warner saying: "That's not governing. The corruption needs to stop." And in former Senator Sherrod Brown's bid to return to the Senate for Ohio, the Democrat has embraced the massive crypto spending against him as a point of favor. "The crypto/data-center crowd are up to $40 million now," Brown, the former chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, said in a recent Pod Save America interview, noting the industry's opposition ads in Ohio were largely bankrolled by a crypto political action committee (Fairshake). "They know I'm going to hold them accountable," Brown said. Fairshake spent tens of millions trying to get him voted out of office two years ago, and the super PAC started major spending again to keep Brown out. As a result, he offers an us-versus-them (regular voters against tech billionaires) narrative on the campaign trail.

items.article_context_en: A new draft targets a fourfold cut in the time it takes Ethereum transactions to become final, which could free up money transfer services tie up while customers’ payments clear. Ethereum researchers want to cut the wait for a transaction to become final from about 16 minutes to roughly four, a change that could make it cheaper to move money between blockchains. Ben Edgington, who coordinates Ethereum’s fast-finality research, filed the draft Wednesday with fellow researchers Francesco D’Amato, Roberto Saltini, Yann Vonlanthen and Mikhail Kalinin. Its initial target is a four-fold improvement, though the design is unfinished and has no activation date. In the current mechanism, a transaction can land in an Ethereum block well before the network treats it as final, the point where validators, the computers that secure the network, commit to never rewriting it. Anyone moving funds off Ethereum has to decide when it’s safe to release money on the other side. But sixteen minutes is a long time to have money in limbo. Say someone sends $10,000 from Ethereum to another network. A transfer service can pay them right away from money it already holds there, then wait to get repaid once the original transaction settles. The customer gets their funds in seconds, and the service has $10,000 tied up until Ethereum is done. Ethereum Foundation research counts that idle money as a real cost for these firms, and a shorter wait lets them reuse it sooner. In practice, a service fronting a steady $1 million an hour would have about $267,000 waiting on repayment with a 16-minute delay. At four minutes, however, that drops to roughly $67,000. Stablecoin providers such as Circle CRCL$85.22, which issues the dollar-pegged USDC, already charges for speed.

items.article_context_en: 22, 2026 Bitcoin’s BTC$84,459.46 share of the crypto market has climbed to the highest level since May, even as prices across the wider market weaken. The cryptocurrency’s dominance rate, its contribution to the total market value of digital assets, reached 60% on Wednesday and remains near that level. The move signals a renewed preference for BTC, with investors favoring the largest cryptocurrency over alternative coins. The rise in dominance comes amid muted price action. Bitcoin slipped below $82,000 on Thursday, reversing Wednesday’s brief push above $84,000. On a seven-day basis, BTC and most other major tokens — including ether ETH$2,490.55, XRP (XRP) and solana (SOL) — were largely little changed to positive, with zcash (ZEC) the only major coin to advance more than 10%. Smaller tokens, however, have seen bigger declines. The CoinDesk Memecoin Index fell more than 5%, while the CoinDesk Computing Select Index dropped 3.5% and the DeFi Select Index lost 2.5%. “The earlier period of crypto outperformance has given way to closer alignment with equities as investors wait for a fresh catalyst within the sector,” Joel Kruger, a market strategist at LMAX Group said in an email. Kruger added that global macroeconomic situation remains the dominant influence, and bitcoin’s scarcity could help it sustain potential jitters in global equity markets. Vikram Subburaj, CEO of India-based Giottus exchange, cautioned against chasing bitcoin rallies, pointing out that exchange-traded funds (ETFs) still lack a consistent bid. “Flows remain volatile, and sustained inflows are needed to confirm a stronger recovery,” he said in an email. “Our advice: Investors should avoid chasing short-term rallies. Consider staggered entries, maintain measured position sizes and monitor ETF flows and Fed signals before increasing exposure.” The Federal Reserve is set to meet on interest-rate policy next week.

Crypto traders are already betting on the largest IPO in India’s history, putting a $110 billion price tag on Indian telecoms giant Jio Platforms as its official three-day public subscription gets underway. The JIOUSDT perpetual contract on Bitget traded near $12 on Thursday. For comparison, the company set a maximum bid price of 1,119 rupees ($11.79) per share. The company is expected to have about 9.21 billion shares outstanding after the sale, valuing it at most around 10.3 trillion rupees ($106 billion). The Bitget contract became available on Oct. Since then, it has traded between $11.48 and $12.24. Volume over the period totals about 369,000 JIO, or roughly $4.4 million, providing a live valuation for a stock that has not yet listed. This isn’t the first time that an impending IPO has found a market on crypto platforms. Perpetual contracts on SpaceX SPCX$145,14 and Cerebras (CBRS), for example, traded on TradeXYZ, a platform on the Hyperliquid network, ahead of their stock market debuts. The contracts show how price discovery for big IPOs is starting to take place on crypto platforms, even before the first share trades. For SpaceX, synthetic perpetual futures on Hyperliquid and Binance traded around $162-$165, implying a valuation of $2.2 trillion. The company’s official IPO valuation was almost 20% lower at $1.8 trillion. It’s worth remembering that a pre-IPO contract is a perpetual future, a bet on price with no expiry date, tied to a company that is not yet on the stock market.

Money is really pouring into fixed-income as stocks extend losses two hours before the close, with the Nasdaq down 2.55% and S&P 500 losing 1.35%. Treasury is now down a whopping 20 basis points on the session to more than a one-month low of 4.945%. The 2-year yield is off 18 basis points to 4.64%. October Fed rate hikes odds are more or less zero at this point, and the odds of no more rate hikes at all this year have soared to 28% from 10%. Of particular note, interest rates are tumbling even as the price of oil has jumped more than 3% today. These markets were nearly perfectly correlated throughout the summer and early fall, with each tick higher in oil resulting in a move upward in rates. That correlation has completely broken of late as traders reassess the idea that higher oil prices are inflationary, and instead consider the deflationary impact of the current energy shock. Bitcoin is near a session low, down 4.2% to $81,100. Ether and XRP are each down more than 5%. “When you think about a bubble, you think about building capacity and then hoping the demand comes,” Blackstone (BX) President Jon Gray told Bloomberg. “With AI, you’re building capacity, and you’re hoping you can keep up with the demand.” “We can’t keep up with customer demand,” he said, referring to Ode, an AI consulting company formed by Blackstone and Anthropic. “Demand is almost parabolic.” He may have a point.

items.article_context_en: Technology shares led regional losses as mixed U.S. earnings unsettled investors and Brent crude climbed above $112 a barrel. Asian stocks tumbled on Thursday, with Chinese equities entering a bear market as technology shares sank and rising oil prices compounded investor concerns. The CSI 300, which tracks the 300 largest stocks traded in Shenzhen and Shanghai, slid 2%, taking the decline from June’s peak to 20%. Other regional benchmarks followed suit. Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell around 3%, South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5%, Taiwan’s benchmark lost 2% and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng declined 3%. Chinese technology shares traded in Hong Kong faced their worst session since President Donald Trump’s April 2025 “Liberation Day” tariff announcement, according to Bloomberg’s David Ingles. According to Ingles, the technology benchmark has fallen more than 40% from its peak, almost erasing gains following Beijing’s Sept. 24 stimulus package, with forward valuations compressed to roughly 13 times earnings. Mixed third-quarter earnings reports from U.S. companies added to the uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence investment. Tesla TSLA$375.50 fell around 3% after the market closed after cutting its capital-spending forecast, while Meta Platforms META$640.98 raised the lower end of its spending guidance. Bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 gave up its advance above $84,000, retreating toward $82,000. Gold fell more than 1% to below $4,100 an ounce, while silver dropped over 3.5% to around $55.
